title: Bangladesh wants solar on 870,000 rooftops. Who pays to put it there?
subtitle: At COP31, Bangladesh said four in five rooftops in its proposed financing plan would need international support. An earlier solar programme shows what affordable credit can change for a family.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Bangladesh wants to put solar panels on roughly 870,000 rooftops by 2030. At the UN climate talks in Antalya on 10 November, Mirana Mahrukh, secretary of Bangladesh’s Power Division, spelled out how much of that ambition depends on help from abroad. Under the financing split she proposed, domestic efforts would support about 174,000 rooftops. The remaining 696,000 would need international cooperation.

Mahrukh set out those figures as Bangladesh endorsed the Global Rooftop Solar Declaration, which aims to double the number of households worldwide using rooftop solar to at least 300 million by 2030. Australia was the first government to sign; Kenya, Nigeria and Vanuatu also backed the declaration in Antalya. The agreement is voluntary. Bangladesh’s figures describe one possible route to 5,500 megawatts of rooftop capacity. They are neither a tally of homes already signed up nor a commitment from lenders.

Bangladesh has done something comparable before. In 2003, when only 27 per cent of its rural population had access to electricity, the government began helping families buy small solar systems instead of waiting for the grid. Local organisations extended credit and serviced the equipment. By 2018, the programme had sold more than 4.1 million systems, reaching about 20 million people, according to the World Bank, which helped finance it. Those sales predate the new pledge.

Muktilia Bhrumo, one of the women who installed a system, described the difference in a focus group recorded in the World Bank’s history of the programme. Her children used to burn their hands on kerosene lamps while she cooked. Sometimes a lamp went out halfway through a meal. Electric light let her choose when to cook, and her elder daughter could study. It is one family’s experience, but it explains why a decision recorded in megawatts can matter long after sunset.

Who owns the roof presents a different problem. A woman renting a flat can pay every electricity bill without having the right to install a single panel. In the Australian state of New South Wales, a grant programme for apartment buildings addressed that split directly: the owners’ corporation had to agree to share installation costs among owners and energy savings proportionately among all residents. Tenants could benefit even though they did not own the equipment.

The declaration asks governments to make financing more affordable, simplify permits and protect consumers. For families considering an offer, the useful figures are closer to home: the deposit, the instalment, the repair bill and, in a shared building, whose electricity account receives the saving. Bangladesh has put a number on the rooftops it hopes to reach. The next figure to watch is how many households can afford to say yes.
